title: V3·NC4 — Memory leaks and heap snapshots
summary: A leak in a garbage-collected runtime is an object that is still reachable and will never be used again. Nothing warns you. This sector is the diagnosis: reading the numbers V8 gives you, taking and parsing heap snapshots, walking retainer paths, and the four caches and registries that produce most real leaks.

# V3·NC4 — Memory leaks and heap snapshots

The service has been up for six days. RSS is at 1.8 GB and climbing about
40 MB a day. Nothing is obviously wrong: latency is fine, no errors, and a
restart fixes it for another six days. Somewhere in there is an object that
someone is still holding on to.

That is what a leak is in a garbage-collected runtime. Not memory the
allocator forgot — V8's collector is thorough — but memory that is *reachable*
from a root and will never be read again. The GC cannot tell the difference
between a cache you meant and an array you forgot to clear, because from its
point of view they are the same graph.

So the skill is not "stop leaking". It is: read the numbers, take a snapshot,
find what is retaining the growth, and change the code that holds it.

## Concept — the numbers, and what each one means

```ts
process.memoryUsage();
// { rss: 108_396_544, heapTotal: 51_912_704, heapUsed: 38_112_408,
//   external: 2_104_312, arrayBuffers: 1_048_576 }
```

- **`heapUsed`** — live JavaScript objects, as of the last measurement. This
  is the number a leak in your own code moves.
- **`heapTotal`** — how much heap V8 has committed. Grows in steps; does not
  shrink eagerly.
- **`external`** — memory held by C++ objects bound to JS objects.
- **`arrayBuffers`** — the part of `external` that is `ArrayBuffer`s and
  `Buffer`s. A "leak" that does not move `heapUsed` is usually here.
- **`rss`** — resident set size, everything the OS has given the process:
  heap, stacks, code, native allocations, fragmentation. It is the number your
  container limit is enforced against, and it lags the heap in both
  directions.

`v8.getHeapStatistics()` adds the number that decides whether you crash:
`heap_size_limit`, which defaults to somewhere near 2 GB on 64-bit and is set
by `--max-old-space-size`. When `used_heap_size` approaches it, V8 collects
harder, and then it aborts with `FATAL ERROR: Reached heap limit`.

**RSS is not heap.** RSS staying high after `heapUsed` falls is normal:
freeing objects makes room inside the heap, but returning pages to the OS is a
separate decision the allocator makes conservatively. Chasing an RSS number
that does not correspond to a heap number wastes days.

## Concept — the shape of the graph

V8's heap is generational. New objects go into a small **new space** and are
collected by a copying scavenger, which is fast and runs constantly; objects
that survive two scavenges are promoted to **old space**, collected by
mark-sweep-compact, which is slower and runs rarely. Large objects skip
straight to **large object space**.

Two practical consequences. First, most garbage never costs you anything — it
dies in new space, and the scavenge cost is proportional to what *survived*,
not to what was allocated. Second, a leak is by definition promoted: it
survived, so it lives in old space, and every major GC has to trace it again.
That is why a leak makes the process slower before it makes it crash.

The healthy pattern in a `heapUsed` graph is a **sawtooth**: allocation climbs,
a major GC drops it back, repeat, with the *bottoms* flat. A leak is the same
sawtooth with the bottoms rising. Reading the minima rather than the raw line
is the single most useful trick in this sector.

## Concept — snapshots

```ts
import v8 from "node:v8";
v8.writeHeapSnapshot("/tmp/heap-1.heapsnapshot");
```

A snapshot is a JSON file describing every object and every edge between them
at one instant. It is big — often larger than the heap it describes — and
taking it stops the world for hundreds of milliseconds to seconds. You can
also arrange to get one automatically: `--heapsnapshot-signal=SIGUSR2` writes
one when you signal the process, and `--heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit=1` writes
one just before the process dies of OOM, which is the only way to see the
state that killed you.

Inside, the format is column-oriented: a `nodes` array of flat integers whose
meaning is given by `meta.node_fields`, an `edges` array likewise, and a
`strings` table that everything indexes into. Chrome DevTools reads it; so can
you, which is what makes leak detection automatable.

The three numbers per object that matter:

- **shallow size** — the object itself;
- **retained size** — everything that would be freed if this object went away;
- **distance** — how many edges from a GC root.

Retained size is the one that finds leaks. A `Map` with a shallow size of 100
bytes retaining 400 MB of request contexts is the whole bug, and shallow size
alone would never point at it.

## Exercise 1 — the numbers, honestly

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `readMemoryReport()` combines `process.memoryUsage()`
and `v8.getHeapStatistics()` into one report with the derived ratios that
actually predict a crash.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc04_memory_leaks ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — reading a snapshot

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `parseSnapshot(json)` decodes the column-oriented
format into typed node records using `meta.node_fields` and the string table.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc04_memory_leaks ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — what is holding the bytes

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `bytesByConstructor(snapshot, k)` aggregates self size
by constructor name and returns the top `k`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc04_memory_leaks ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — the retainer path

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `retainerPath(snapshot, nodeId)` finds the shortest
path from a GC root to a node and names every edge along the way.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc04_memory_leaks ex4
```

## Exercise 5 — the diff

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `diffSnapshots(before, after, options)` reports which
constructors grew, by how much, and which of them clear the noise floor.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc04_memory_leaks ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — a cache that cannot leak

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `createLruCache({ maxBytes, sizeOf })` evicts by byte
budget with exact accounting, including on overwrite.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc04_memory_leaks ex6
```

## Exercise 7 — subscriptions that go away

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `createRegistry()` hands out an unsubscribe function,
is provably empty afterwards, and stores per-subscriber metadata in a
`WeakMap`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc04_memory_leaks ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — is this a leak?

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `classifyTrend(samples)` reads a series of `heapUsed`
readings and returns `"stable"`, `"sawtooth"` or `"growing"` from the minima,
not the peaks.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc04_memory_leaks ex8
```

## Challenge — a leak detector

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. `findSuspects(before, after, options)` combines
the diff, the retainer path and a growth threshold into a ranked report.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc04_memory_leaks challenge
```

## Review — weak references and their limits

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. `createLivenessTracker()` uses `WeakRef` to count
what is still alive, and documents exactly what `FinalizationRegistry` does
not promise.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc04_memory_leaks review1
```

# Reading - node/v3nc04_memory_leaks

Finding a leak is an evidence problem, not a cleverness problem. The tools
give you a graph; the skill is knowing which number to sort by and which
object to be suspicious of.

## Notes

**Reachability is the definition.** If a root — the global object, an active
stack frame, a live closure, a module scope — can reach an object, it stays.
Every leak in Node is one of five roots holding one of five collection types:
a module-level `Map`/`Set`/array, an emitter's listener list, a timer's
closure, a promise that never settles, or a native handle.

**`heapUsed` is a sample, not a truth.** Read immediately after a major GC it
is the live set; read halfway through an allocation burst it is live plus
garbage. That is why trends are read from the minima: the minimum of a window
approximates "what survived the last collection".

**Three snapshots, not one.** The technique that works: snapshot, exercise the
suspected path N times, snapshot, exercise again, snapshot. Compare 2 with 3
rather than 1 with 2 — the first comparison is polluted by lazy
initialisation, JIT warm-up and one-time caches. What appears in both diffs is
the leak.

**Retained size is the sort key.** Shallow size finds you a million small
strings; retained size finds you the one object whose removal frees them all.
DevTools' "Comparison" view sorted by delta retained size is where you should
be looking within thirty seconds of opening a snapshot.

**`external` and `arrayBuffers` are a separate budget.** A `Buffer` is a small
JS object pointing at memory outside the heap. Ten thousand retained 1 MB
buffers barely move `heapUsed` and will absolutely get your container OOM
killed, because RSS counts them and the heap limit does not.

**`--max-old-space-size` postpones, it does not fix.** Raising the limit buys
time proportional to the increase and makes each major GC more expensive. It
is a legitimate mitigation while you find the bug and a terrible permanent
answer.

**OOM kill and heap-limit abort are different failures.** V8 aborting with
"Reached heap limit" prints a stack and can write a snapshot first. The Linux
OOM killer sending `SIGKILL` prints nothing anywhere in your process, and the
only evidence is `dmesg` or the pod's `Reason: OOMKilled`. If your crash left
no trace, it was the kernel.

## ex1 — the report you actually want

Raw `memoryUsage()` is five numbers with no thresholds. The derived ratio
`used_heap_size / heap_size_limit` is the one that predicts a crash, and
`rss - heapTotal` approximates everything that is *not* the JS heap — buffers,
native modules, fragmentation — which is where you look when the heap is
healthy and the container is not.

## ex2 — the format

Column-oriented storage is why a snapshot of a 500 MB heap is not 5 GB of
JSON: nodes are flat integers, and `meta.node_fields` tells you the stride.
Decoding it yourself once removes all the mystery from the DevTools UI, and it
is the prerequisite for any automated leak check in CI.

## ex3 — aggregation

Grouping by constructor name is the first question anyone asks of a snapshot:
*what is there a lot of?* The answer is usually `(string)`, `Object` and
`Array`, which is why the useful version filters to your own class names and
sorts by total rather than count.

## ex4 — the path

A retainer path is a breadth-first search from the roots, and BFS specifically:
the *shortest* path is the one that names the responsible variable, while a
depth-first walk can hand you a forty-step cycle through unrelated objects.
The edge names along the path — a property name, an array index, a closure
variable — are the line of code you are looking for.

## ex5 — the diff

Two summaries, one subtraction, and a threshold. The threshold is the
interesting part: every heap grows a little between snapshots, so a detector
with no noise floor reports fifty suspects and is ignored. A rule like "grew
by more than 5% and more than 1 MB" produces a list you can read.

## ex6 — bounded by construction

An LRU with a byte budget cannot leak, and the exercise's real content is the
accounting: subtract the old size before adding the new one on overwrite, or
the recorded total drifts above the real one until the cache evicts everything
and still believes it is full.

## ex7 — the unsubscribe

Returning a disposer rather than requiring the caller to keep the function
identity is the API that makes cleanup possible. The `WeakMap` is the second
half: keyed by the subscriber object, entries disappear when the subscriber
does, with no explicit deletion at all.

## ex8 — reading a trend

Minima over a window, then a slope. The naive version fits a line through the
raw samples and reports "growing" for a healthy sawtooth whose window happened
to end mid-allocation. Sampling on a fixed interval and taking each window's
minimum removes almost all of that noise.

## challenge — the detector

Diff, threshold, rank, and explain. The "explain" is what makes it useful: a
report saying `SessionContext grew 12,400 objects, retained by Map in
sessions.ts` is a ticket, and a report saying `Object: +12,400` is a shrug.

## review1 — weak, and honest about it

`WeakRef` lets you observe without retaining. `FinalizationRegistry` tells you
*maybe*, *later*, *possibly never* — it is not a destructor, it does not run
at process exit, and building resource cleanup on it produces bugs that appear
only under memory pressure. The exercise makes you write the caveat down.

## Further reading

- [`v8` — Node.js API docs](https://nodejs.org/api/v8.html) — `getHeapStatistics`, `writeHeapSnapshot`, `getHeapSnapshot`.
- [Heap snapshot format](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/main/include/v8-profiler.h) — the source of truth for `meta.node_fields`.
- [Chrome DevTools: record heap snapshots](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/memory-problems/heap-snapshots) — shallow versus retained size, the comparison view.
- [`WeakRef` — MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/WeakRef) — including the "avoid if you can" advice from the spec authors.
- [`FinalizationRegistry` — MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/FinalizationRegistry) — the list of things it does not guarantee.

# V3·NC4 — Memory leaks and heap snapshots (archive)

## The five leaks that account for most of them

**1. A module-scope collection with no bound.**

```ts
const cache = new Map<string, Result>();          // never evicted
export function get(key: string) { ... cache.set(key, value); ... }
```

Module scope is a GC root for the life of the process. Every entry is
permanent. This is the most common leak in Node by a wide margin, and the fix
is a bound — an LRU with a byte or entry budget, or a TTL sweep.

**2. Listeners on a long-lived emitter.**

```ts
pool.on("error", () => cleanupThisRequest());     // one per request, never removed
```

The emitter holds the closure, the closure holds the request context, the
context holds the parsed body. Node's `MaxListenersExceededWarning` at eleven
listeners exists precisely to catch this, and the fix is `off` in a `finally`
or `{ signal }` on `addEventListener`.

**3. A timer that captures.**

```ts
setInterval(() => report(bigThing), 60_000);      // bigThing is immortal
```

An uncleared interval is a root. `unref()` does not help — it affects whether
the loop stays alive, not reachability.

**4. Promises that never settle.**

Every pending promise retains its continuation, which retains its closure. Ten
thousand requests waiting on a service that never replies is ten thousand
retained contexts, and the symptom looks like a memory leak because it is one.

**5. Buffers.**

`external`/`arrayBuffers` memory does not count against the V8 heap limit but
does count against the container. A queue of 1 MB buffers is a 500 MB RSS
problem that a heap snapshot will show as a few thousand tiny objects.

## Worked example — the three-snapshot technique

```ts
import v8 from "node:v8";

async function measure(exercise: () => Promise<void>): Promise<void> {
  await exercise();                                  // warm up: lazy init, JIT
  global.gc?.();                                     // node --expose-gc
  v8.writeHeapSnapshot("/tmp/a.heapsnapshot");

  for (let i = 0; i < 100; i++) await exercise();
  global.gc?.();
  v8.writeHeapSnapshot("/tmp/b.heapsnapshot");

  for (let i = 0; i < 100; i++) await exercise();
  global.gc?.();
  v8.writeHeapSnapshot("/tmp/c.heapsnapshot");
}
```

Compare B with C, not A with B. The first hundred iterations populate caches,
compile functions and allocate one-time structures; anything that grows
*again* in the second hundred is the leak. Forcing a GC before each snapshot
matters too — otherwise you are diffing garbage that had not been collected
yet and every constructor looks like it grew.

In production you cannot `--expose-gc` or stop the world for two seconds on
demand. The equivalent is `--heapsnapshot-signal=SIGUSR2`, a `kill -USR2` at
two points an hour apart, and the same comparison offline.

## Worked example — sizing the evidence

```ts
const before = process.memoryUsage().heapUsed;
for (let i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) suspect();
const after = process.memoryUsage().heapUsed;
console.log(`${((after - before) / 100_000).toFixed(1)} bytes per call`);
```

Crude and often decisive. A leak of 40 bytes per call is invisible in a
snapshot diff of a small test and obvious here, and "bytes per call" times
"calls per day" is the number that tells you whether it matters at all. Some
leaks are real and irrelevant: 40 bytes on an endpoint called twice a day is
30 KB a year.

## Worked example — the leak that is not in the heap

```ts
const pending = new Map<string, Buffer>();

app.post("/upload", async (req, res) => {
  const body = await readBody(req);          // a 5 MB Buffer
  pending.set(req.headers["x-upload-id"] as string, body);
  res.status(202).end();
});
```

Two hundred uploads later, RSS is up by a gigabyte and a heap snapshot shows
almost nothing: two hundred small `Buffer` objects with a self size of about a
hundred bytes each. The five megabytes per entry live in `external` memory,
outside the V8 heap, invisible to `heapUsed` and uncounted by
`--max-old-space-size`.

The diagnostic is `process.memoryUsage().arrayBuffers` climbing while
`heapUsed` is flat. The fix is the same as for any unbounded map — a TTL, a
byte budget, or storing the payload somewhere that is not the process — but
you will never find it by staring at a snapshot's constructor list.

This is the single most useful distinction in this sector: **objects leak in
the heap, payloads leak in `external`, and they need different instruments.**
A service that streams, compresses, hashes or proxies is much more likely to
have the second kind.

## Common mistakes

- **Chasing RSS.** RSS includes native allocations and fragmentation and lags
  the heap. Confirm the growth in `heapUsed` before you open a snapshot.
- **Diffing the first two snapshots.** Lazy initialisation looks exactly like
  a leak.
- **Snapshotting without forcing a GC.** Uncollected garbage inflates every
  constructor.
- **Sorting by shallow size.** Finds symptoms, not causes.
- **Assuming `WeakMap` fixes everything.** It only helps when the *key* is the
  thing whose lifetime you want to follow. A `WeakMap` keyed by a string is a
  `Map`.
- **Relying on `FinalizationRegistry` for cleanup.** It may never run.
- **Raising `--max-old-space-size` as the fix.** Slower GCs, later crash.
- **Ignoring `arrayBuffers`.** The one number that can OOM a container while
  the heap looks perfect.
- **Removing listeners with a new arrow function.** `off` matches by identity.
- **Forgetting that closures capture the whole scope.** A callback that uses
  one field of a 10 MB object can retain the whole object, depending on what
  else the enclosing scope references.

## Interview answer

*"How would you debug a memory leak in a Node service?"*

First I confirm it is a heap leak: `heapUsed` rising across the *minima* of
the sawtooth, not just RSS, since RSS includes native memory and
fragmentation. If it is `external`/`arrayBuffers` instead, I am looking at
buffers and streams rather than objects. Then I get snapshots — in production
via `--heapsnapshot-signal=SIGUSR2`, locally with `writeHeapSnapshot` around a
repeated exercise of the suspect path — and I take three, comparing the second
with the third so lazy initialisation does not pollute the diff. In the
comparison view I sort by delta retained size, pick the constructor that keeps
growing, and follow its retainer path back to a root; the edge names tell me
which variable is holding it. The fixes are nearly always the same handful:
bound the cache, remove the listener, clear the timer, settle the promise. If
I need a safety net while I look, `--max-old-space-size` and a scheduled
restart buy time, but I would not call that a fix.

## Check yourself

1. Define a memory leak in a garbage-collected runtime.
2. Why can RSS stay high after `heapUsed` drops?
3. What does `arrayBuffers` measure, and why can it OOM a container that the
   heap limit would never catch?
4. Why compare the second and third snapshots rather than the first and
   second?
5. What is the difference between shallow and retained size, and which finds
   leaks?
6. Why is a BFS the right search for a retainer path?
7. What does the sawtooth pattern look like when it is healthy, and when it is
   not?
8. Name five common sources of retention in a Node service.
9. When does a `WeakMap` actually help?
10. What does `FinalizationRegistry` *not* guarantee?
11. What is the effect of raising `--max-old-space-size`, in both directions?
12. How can you tell a V8 heap-limit abort from a kernel OOM kill after the
    fact?
13. Why does a leak make a process slower before it makes it crash?

# What the collector can and cannot know

## Reachability, and the honest definition of a leak

V8's garbage collector answers exactly one question: starting from the roots,
which objects can I reach? Everything reachable stays; everything else is
freed. The roots are the global object, the current stack (every local
variable in every active frame), the handles held by native code, and a few
internal structures.

That is a complete and correct algorithm for "memory that can still be used".
It is not an algorithm for "memory that will still be used", and it cannot be,
because that is undecidable. So the definition of a leak is a human one: an
object the program can still reach and never will.

This is why leaks in Node are always someone's data structure. There is no
allocator bug to find. Some collection, somewhere, is holding a reference, and
the entire diagnostic process is finding out which.

## Generations, and why leaks cost speed

V8 splits the heap. New allocations go into **new space** (a few megabytes,
split into two semi-spaces) and are collected by Scavenger, a copying
collector: live objects are copied to the other semi-space, everything else is
abandoned wholesale. Cost is proportional to what *survived*, which for
typical JavaScript is a tiny fraction — this is why allocating short-lived
objects in a loop is much cheaper than intuition suggests.

Objects that survive two scavenges are promoted to **old space**, collected by
Mark-Compact: mark everything reachable, sweep the rest, occasionally compact
to reduce fragmentation. This is the expensive collector, and V8 works hard to
run it incrementally and concurrently so the pauses stay small.

Now the consequence for leaks. A leaked object is, by construction, one that
survived — so it is in old space, and every major GC has to trace it and its
entire subgraph again. A heap with 400 MB of leaked session objects pays for
those 400 MB on every major collection, forever. The service gets slower and
its GC pauses get longer weeks before it runs out of memory, which is why "the
p99 has been creeping up" and "we restart it every Sunday" are usually the
same bug.

There is also **large object space**, for allocations above roughly half a
page's worth (about 128 KB in practice), which are never copied. Big buffers
and long strings land there and are freed only by a major GC — one reason
buffer-heavy services show a lumpier memory profile than object-heavy ones.

## The snapshot format, from the inside

A `.heapsnapshot` is JSON with a deliberately boring structure:

```json
{
  "snapshot": { "meta": { "node_fields": ["type", "name", "id", "self_size", "edge_count", ...],
                          "node_types": [[...]], "edge_fields": [...] },
                "node_count": 1200000, "edge_count": 4800000 },
  "nodes": [ 9, 1, 1, 0, 3, 0, 0, ... ],
  "edges": [ 1, 2, 24, ... ],
  "strings": ["", "(GC roots)", "Object", "SessionContext", ...]
}
```

Every node is `node_fields.length` consecutive integers in the flat `nodes`
array; `name` is an index into `strings`; `type` is an index into
`node_types[0]`. Edges are the same idea, and each node's edges are the next
`edge_count` entries of the edge array, walked in node order — so computing
"which edges belong to node i" means summing every previous node's edge count,
which is why every parser builds a prefix-sum index first.

The format is column-oriented for size: repeated strings appear once, and
integers pack better than objects. It is still enormous — a 500 MB heap
produces a snapshot of a similar order, and `JSON.parse` on it needs more
memory than the file. Parsing a production snapshot on your laptop can require
`--max-old-space-size=8192`, which is a memorable irony.

## Taking a snapshot without making things worse

`v8.writeHeapSnapshot()` stops the world for the duration — hundreds of
milliseconds for a small heap, several seconds for a large one — and writes a
file at least as large as the live heap. On a production instance, that is a
latency spike and a disk write you must have planned for.

The flags exist to make it survivable. `--heapsnapshot-signal=SIGUSR2` lets
you take one on demand from outside the process, which is the standard way to
grab a pair an hour apart. `--heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit=N` writes up to N
snapshots as the heap approaches its limit, giving you the state that killed
the process — the single highest-value flag in this list, because an OOM crash
otherwise leaves nothing to inspect. `v8.setHeapSnapshotNearHeapLimit(n)` is
the programmatic equivalent.

For a lighter touch there is sampling: `--heap-prof` writes an allocation
profile that tells you which *call sites* allocated, at a few percent
overhead, without ever stopping the world. It answers "who allocates" rather
than "who retains", which is a different and sometimes more useful question.

## Weak references, and why they are a last resort

`WeakMap` and `WeakSet` hold their keys weakly: an entry disappears when the
key is collected, with no bookkeeping from you. That is genuinely the right
answer for per-object metadata — an id for a request object, a parsed form for
a config object — and it is the only weak construct that is easy to use
correctly.

`WeakRef` and `FinalizationRegistry`, added in ES2021, are different. The
proposal's own documentation advises avoiding them, and the reasons are worth
carrying:

- a `WeakRef`'s target may be collected at any time between reads, so code
  that dereferences twice can get an object and then `undefined`;
- V8 keeps a `WeakRef`'s target alive until the end of the current job, which
  makes behaviour depend on turn boundaries;
- a `FinalizationRegistry` callback runs *maybe*, *eventually*, and never at
  all if the process exits first — so closing a file handle from one is a bug
  that appears as descriptor exhaustion under low memory pressure;
- finalizers can resurrect objects and are not run in any guaranteed order.

The rule that survives: use `WeakMap` freely, use `WeakRef` for caches where
losing the entry is harmless, and never let a `FinalizationRegistry` be the
only thing that releases a resource.

## Closures, and the scope you did not mean to keep

One retention mechanism deserves its own section because it is invisible in
the source. A closure captures its enclosing scope, and V8's context objects
are shared between all closures created in the same scope. So this:

```ts
function handle(request: Request) {
  const body = request.body;                 // 10 MB
  const id = request.id;
  return {
    log: () => console.log(id),              // only uses `id`
    parse: () => JSON.parse(body),
  };
}
```

can retain `body` for as long as *either* closure lives, because both share
one context. Keep the `log` function in a long-lived map and you have retained
ten megabytes to print a string. V8's optimiser does eliminate variables that
no closure references at all, but it cannot help when a sibling closure in the
same scope still uses them.

The fix is boring and effective: narrow the scope. Extract the long-lived
callback into its own function taking only what it needs, or null out the
large binding once you are done with it. In a snapshot this shows up as an
edge named `body in handle` pointing from a `(closure)` node, which is exactly
why ex4 asks you to keep the edge names.

## When not to investigate

- **When the growth is bounded and intentional.** A cache that grows to 200 MB
  and stops is not a leak. Confirm the plateau before spending a day.
- **When the numbers are noise.** A few megabytes over an hour on a service
  that restarts daily is not worth a snapshot.
- **When it is `external`, not heap.** Different tools entirely: look at
  stream lifetimes, `Buffer` pooling and native modules.
- **When the fix is a restart and the service is stateless.** Unpopular, but a
  scheduled restart is a legitimate mitigation for a third-party leak you
  cannot patch. Document it as a mitigation, not as a fix, or it becomes
  permanent by silence.

The one thing that is never right is guessing. Snapshots exist so that "I
think it might be the cache" can become "the cache retains 312 MB across two
snapshots and here is the path", and that difference is the entire sector.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two sources, because neither is complete. `process.memoryUsage()` knows about
RSS and external memory; `v8.getHeapStatistics()` knows about the limit that
will actually kill you. The report exists to put them next to each other.

## Hint 2

```ts
import v8 from "node:v8";
const { heap_size_limit, used_heap_size } = v8.getHeapStatistics();
```

Note the snake_case: these come straight from V8's C++ struct, and they are
one of the few places in Node's API where that shows. `used_heap_size` and
`process.memoryUsage().heapUsed` are the same number measured a moment apart.

## Hint 3

Compute `heapPressure` from `heapUsed / heapLimit` and clamp `nonHeapRss` at
zero — RSS can legitimately be smaller than `heapTotal` on a system that has
paged out memory the process committed but never touched.

The decision left to you: whether `status` should consider `nonHeapRss` at
all. A process at 30% heap pressure and 3 GB of buffers is in trouble that
this ratio cannot see.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter from the alert you would page someone with. "Memory is high" is not
actionable; "heap pressure 0.93, and the last three samples were 0.89, 0.91,
0.93" tells the on-call engineer they have minutes and which flag to reach
for.

Designing the numbers around the decision is the difference between telemetry
and noise.

## Hint 2

Understand what the limit is before you divide by it. `heap_size_limit`
defaults to roughly 2 GB on 64-bit Node (it varies with version and available
memory) and is set by `--max-old-space-size` in megabytes. Crossing it does
not throw — V8 aborts the process with `FATAL ERROR: Reached heap limit
Allocation failed`, which no `try`/`catch` will see.

That is why the ratio is worth exporting: it is the only warning you get.

## Hint 3

`nonHeapRss` deserves a comment in your code explaining that it is an
approximation. RSS includes the heap, the stacks, the executable, mapped
files, native allocations and fragmentation; subtracting `heapTotal` gives a
useful trend line and a meaningless absolute number. Trends are what you want
from it anyway: a `nonHeapRss` that climbs while the heap is flat means
buffers, native modules or descriptors, and none of those show up in a heap
snapshot.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start by getting a real snapshot to look at, because the format is much less
intimidating once you have seen one:

```ts
import v8 from "node:v8";
v8.writeHeapSnapshot("/tmp/x.heapsnapshot");
```

Then `head -c 2000` it. You will see `snapshot.meta` with the field names, a
long run of small integers, and a string table at the end.

## Hint 2

The thing that will surprise you is the size. A snapshot of a modest heap is
tens of megabytes of JSON, and `JSON.parse` of it needs several times the
file's size in heap — which means the tool you write to analyse a leak can
itself run out of memory. Production snapshot analysis routinely needs
`node --max-old-space-size=8192`.

That is a real constraint on the design: you cannot afford to build an object
per edge for a large file.

## Hint 3

Note why the format is column-oriented at all. A snapshot with three million
nodes stored as objects would be JSON with three million repetitions of every
key name. Flat integer arrays plus a shared string table make the file roughly
an order of magnitude smaller and parse much faster — the same reason columnar
formats exist in analytics.

Understanding that also tells you what it costs: nothing can be read without
the `meta` header, and a truncated file is completely unrecoverable.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 3 — what is holding the bytes

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export interface ConstructorTotal { name: string; count: number; selfSize: number; }

export function bytesByConstructor(
  snapshot: { nodes: Array<{ name: string; type: string; selfSize: number }> },
  options?: { top?: number; types?: readonly string[] },
): ConstructorTotal[]
```

Group nodes by `name`, summing `selfSize` and counting instances. Return the
top `options.top` (default 10) sorted by `selfSize` descending, with ties
broken by `name` ascending so the output is stable.

`options.types` filters to those node types (default: `["object", "closure"]`)
— because without a filter, every snapshot's answer is `(string)`, `Array` and
`(system)`, which is true and useless.

```ts
bytesByConstructor(snapshot, { top: 2 });
// [ { name: "SessionContext", count: 12400, selfSize: 5_952_000 },
//   { name: "Order", count: 800, selfSize: 76_800 } ]
```

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc04_memory_leaks ex3
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter from the limitation, because it is the honest framing. Self size is what
the object itself occupies: a `Map` with a million entries has a self size of
a few dozen bytes. Sorting by self size therefore finds you the *contents* of
a leak — a million `SessionContext` objects — but never the container that is
holding them.

Chrome DevTools computes retained size with a dominator-tree algorithm over
the whole graph, which is genuinely more work than this exercise. Knowing that
you are using the cheap approximation is the point.

## Hint 2

Now why the type filter earns its place. Run the aggregation with no filter on
any real snapshot and the top entries are `(string)`, `(array)`, `(system)`
and `(compiled code)`. All of that is true; none of it names a line in your
codebase. Filtering to objects and closures makes the report show *your*
classes, which is what a leak hunt needs.

## Hint 3

Think about what a good report looks like at the end. Two constructors with
identical byte totals but counts of 12,400 and 3 are completely different
bugs: the first is a container that never evicts, the second is three enormous
objects. Keeping `count` alongside `selfSize` costs one integer and answers
that question immediately, which is why the interface has both.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 4 — the retainer path

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export interface Graph {
  nodes: Array<{ index: number; id: number; name: string; edgeCount: number; firstEdge: number }>;
  edges: Array<{ toNode: number; name: string }>;   // toNode is a node index
}

export function retainerPath(graph: Graph, targetId: number): string[] | undefined
```

Find the **shortest** path from node index 0 (the GC roots node) to the node
with `id === targetId`, and return it as readable steps:

```
["(GC roots)", "sessions", "Map", "table", "Array", "0", "SessionContext"]
```

— the root's name, then for each step the edge name followed by the node name
it reaches. Return `undefined` when the target does not exist or is
unreachable. The graph may contain cycles.

```ts
retainerPath(graph, 42);   // ["(GC roots)", "cache", "Map", "value", "Entry"]
```

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc04_memory_leaks ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Breadth-first, not depth-first, and the reason is not performance. BFS returns
the shortest path, and the shortest retainer path is the one that names the
variable actually responsible. A DFS can hand you a forty-step route through
unrelated objects that happens to arrive at the same place.

## Hint 2

Standard BFS with a parent map, then walk it backwards:

```ts
const parent = new Map<number, { from: number; edge: string }>();
const queue = [0];
const seen = new Set([0]);
while (queue.length > 0) {
  const current = queue.shift()!;
  // ... for each outgoing edge, if unseen: record parent, enqueue
}
```

The `seen` set is what makes cycles terminate. Without it, a heap graph — which
is full of cycles — will loop forever.

## Hint 3

Each node's outgoing edges are `graph.edges` from `firstEdge` to
`firstEdge + edgeCount`. Build the path by following parents from the target
back to the root, then reverse it, interleaving edge names and node names.

The decision left to you: `queue.shift()` is O(n) on a large array. For a
three-million-node graph that matters — consider an index cursor instead, and
say why in a comment.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from what the answer is *for*. The path is a sentence: "the GC roots
hold `sessions`, which is a `Map`, whose table holds an `Array`, whose element
0 is a `SessionContext`." That sentence names a variable in a file, and that
variable is the fix.

Every step you drop from the output makes the sentence less actionable, which
is why the edge names matter as much as the node names.

## Hint 2

The edge names are more informative than they look. In a real snapshot they
are property names (`sessions`), array indices (`0`), closure variable names
(`context in handleRequest`), and internal names in parentheses. A path
containing `context in handleRequest` tells you a closure captured something,
which is a different fix from a property assignment.

## Hint 3

Consider the case the exercise makes you handle: the target is unreachable.
In a real snapshot that should be impossible — every node in the file was
reachable when the snapshot was taken — so `undefined` means your traversal is
wrong, most likely because you used the node *id* where an *index* was
expected.

Node ids are stable across snapshots (that is what makes diffing possible) and
node indices are positions in this file. Mixing them up is the single most
common bug when writing snapshot tooling.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Index `before` by name, walk `after`, subtract. The thresholds are the part
that turns a diff into a report: without them you get every constructor in the
heap, most of which moved by a few hundred bytes for reasons nobody can act
on.

## Hint 2

Both conditions have to hold, and each catches something the other misses:

- an absolute floor rejects a `Map` that grew from 40 bytes to 4 KB — a 100x
  ratio that costs nothing;
- a ratio floor rejects a 200 MB cache that grew by 2 MB — a big absolute
  number that is normal operation.

That is the whole design of a useful alert: relative *and* absolute.

## Hint 3

`ratio` when `before.selfSize` is 0 should be `Infinity`, and `Infinity`
compares correctly against any `minRatio`, so no special case is needed in the
filter. Handle it in the computation, not in the branch.

The decision left to you: whether shrinking constructors belong in the output.
The type says `Growth`, but a report that shows a big drop next to a big rise
often explains both.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from the report nobody reads. A leak detector that prints fifty
lines is worse than no detector, because it trains people to close the tab.
The thresholds exist to make the output short enough that someone looks at
every line.

Pick defaults you can defend out loud: "more than a megabyte and more than 5%"
is defensible; "anything that grew" is not.

## Hint 2

Then the sampling discipline the numbers assume. Diffing snapshot 1 with
snapshot 2 catches every lazy initialisation, every cache warm-up and every
compiled function as "growth". Comparing 2 with 3 — after the same workload
has run once — leaves only what grows *repeatedly*.

Your function cannot enforce that, but the doc comment can say it, and saying
it is what makes the tool usable by someone who has not read this sector.

## Hint 3

Consider what to do about constructor names you cannot act on. `Object`,
`Array` and `(string)` will often top the list even after filtering, because
the leaked objects are plain. A production version of this tool usually keeps
an allow-list of your own class names, or joins the diff with the retainer
path from ex4 so that even a growth of anonymous objects points at a named
container.

That join is what the challenge asks for.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A JavaScript `Map` iterates in insertion order, and that is enough to build an
LRU without a linked list: to mark a key as recently used, `delete` it and
`set` it again, which moves it to the end.

`map.keys().next().value` is then the least recently used key.

## Hint 2

The accounting is where the bugs are:

```ts
const existing = store.get(key);
if (existing !== undefined) bytes -= sizeOf(existing);
bytes += size;
store.set(key, value);
```

Forgetting the subtraction on overwrite makes `bytes` drift permanently above
the truth, and a cache that believes it is full evicts everything and then
keeps evicting.

## Hint 3

Eviction is a `while`, not an `if`: one large insert can require evicting
several small entries. And the oversized-value rule needs to come first, or
you will evict the entire cache to make room for something you then refuse to
store.

The decision left to you: whether `sizeOf` is called once per `set` or every
time you need the size. Calling it repeatedly is correct only if it is pure
and cheap — and if the value is mutated after insertion, neither version is
right.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter from the failure this design eliminates. An unbounded `Map` at module
scope is the most common leak in Node, and it is never written as a mistake —
it is written as a cache, by someone who assumed the key space was small. User
ids, URLs, request bodies and error messages all look bounded until the day
they are not.

A cache with a budget cannot become that bug, no matter what the key space
does.

## Hint 2

Then the honest limitation of byte budgets: `sizeOf` is an estimate. Nobody
can cheaply measure a JavaScript object's true retained footprint, so real
caches count string lengths, buffer byte lengths, or a fixed cost per entry.
Being 30% wrong consistently is fine; the budget still bounds you.

What is *not* fine is a `sizeOf` that changes for the same value, which is
exactly what happens if callers mutate cached objects. Document it.

## Hint 3

Consider the interaction with the rest of this sector. A bounded cache still
shows up in a heap snapshot as a large retainer — it is *supposed* to. The
skill from ex3 and ex5 is distinguishing "large and stable" from "large and
growing", and a cache with a budget produces exactly the first pattern: it
climbs to its bound and flattens.

That plateau is what tells you to stop investigating, and it is the reason
`bytes` is part of the public interface rather than a private detail.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Returning a disposer is the API decision that makes cleanup possible at all.
The alternative — `off(handler)` — requires the caller to keep the exact
function identity, and the moment someone passes an inline arrow the
subscription is unremovable.

## Hint 2

Give each subscription its own identity so the same subscriber can appear
twice:

```ts
const entry = { subscriber, handler };
entries.add(entry);
return () => { entries.delete(entry); };
```

A `Set` of entry objects handles idempotent unsubscribe for free: deleting
something that is already gone is a no-op that returns `false`.

## Hint 3

For `publish`, iterate over a **copy** of the set. A handler that unsubscribes
during dispatch mutates the collection you are iterating, and the surviving
handlers silently stop being called — the same bug that makes the real
`EventEmitter` clone its listener array before dispatch.

The decision left to you: what to do with a handler that throws. Swallowing
hides bugs; rethrowing means one bad subscriber breaks everyone. Pick, and say
why.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter from the leak. A long-lived emitter with one listener added per request
grows forever: the emitter holds the closure, the closure holds the request
context, the context holds the parsed body and the response. Memory climbs by
a few kilobytes per request, which is invisible for a day and fatal in a week.

`MaxListenersExceededWarning` at eleven listeners exists to catch exactly
this, and most teams silence it instead of reading it.

## Hint 2

Now the `WeakMap`, and specifically when it helps. It helps when the *key* is
the object whose lifetime you want the entry to follow: metadata about a
subscriber, keyed by the subscriber. It does nothing at all when the key is a
string — `new WeakMap()` with string keys is not even legal — and it does not
make the *values* weak, so a `WeakMap` whose values point back at their keys
retains everything.

That last one is a real bug pattern and worth a sentence in your comments.

## Hint 3

Think about what "provably empty" means for a test. `size === 0` is the
observable version, and it is the right assertion because it does not depend
on the garbage collector running. Any test that asserts "the object was
collected" is asking V8 for a guarantee it does not make, and it will be flaky
on exactly the machine you cannot debug.

Assert on your own bookkeeping; leave the GC out of your test suite.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The reason to use minima is worth stating before you code it. A `heapUsed`
sample taken mid-allocation includes garbage that has not been collected yet.
The minimum of a window is the closest cheap approximation to "the live set
after the last major GC", and only that number tells you whether the *live*
data is growing.

## Hint 2

Least squares on `(index, value)` pairs is four sums:

```ts
const n = minima.length;
const sumX = ..., sumY = ..., sumXY = ..., sumXX = ...;
const slope = (n * sumXY - sumX * sumY) / (n * sumXX - sumX * sumX);
```

The denominator is zero only when every x is identical, which cannot happen
for consecutive indices with `n >= 2` — but write the guard anyway, because
`0/0` is `NaN` and `NaN` comparisons are all false, which turns a bug into a
silent "stable".

## Hint 3

Drop the incomplete final window rather than taking the minimum of a partial
one: a window with two samples is systematically higher than a window with
five, which tilts the slope upward and reports a leak that does not exist.

The decision left to you: whether "growing" should require the slope to be
positive across *every* pair of consecutive minima as well as on average. The
stricter rule has fewer false positives and misses slow leaks.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter from the two wrong answers this function exists to avoid.

A detector that alerts on the raw series alerts every time a burst of traffic
allocates — which is every day, so people mute it. A detector that only looks
at the first and last sample gets whatever the sampling happened to catch. In
both cases the tool is discarded within a week.

Statistics over the minima is the cheapest thing that survives contact with a
real service.

## Hint 2

Now what the analysis cannot see. A leak that grows in `arrayBuffers` does not
move `heapUsed` at all, and this function will report "stable" for a process
that is minutes from an OOM kill. So a real monitor runs the same
classification over three series — `heapUsed`, `external` and `rss` — and
reports which of them is growing.

Noticing what your instrument is blind to is most of the skill in
observability, which is the next sector but one.

## Hint 3

Consider the sampling interval, since the function assumes but does not check
it. Samples one second apart with major GCs every thirty seconds means most
windows never contain a post-GC minimum, and every window's minimum is
inflated. Samples one minute apart over an hour is 60 points, and windows of
5 give 12 minima, which is enough for a slope you can believe.

Rule of thumb: your window should span at least one full GC cycle. If you do
not know your GC cycle, `--trace-gc` for a minute tells you.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three functions you have already written, plus a join. Write the pipeline as
three named steps rather than one loop — diff, locate, explain — because the
next person to read it will want to run just one of them.

## Hint 2

The join is "for this constructor name, which node do I explain?" The largest
instance is a good default heuristic:

```ts
const biggest = graph.nodes
  .filter((node) => node.name === suspect.name)
  .reduce((a, b) => (b.selfSize > a.selfSize ? b : a));
```

It is a heuristic and not a truth — the largest instance may be retained
differently from the other 12,000 — so say so in a comment rather than
implying the path explains them all.

## Hint 3

BFS over a large graph is the expensive part, and you are doing one per
suspect. Since every search starts from node 0, one BFS computing the parent
map for the whole graph and reused for every suspect is strictly better.

The decision left to you: whether to do that optimisation now. Measure the
suspect count first — for five suspects it does not matter, and premature
generality is its own cost.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enter from the ticket you want to file. The output of this tool should be
copy-pasteable into an issue: *"`SessionContext` grew from 1.2 MB to 48 MB
(40x, +12,400 instances) between snapshots; the largest instance is retained
by (GC roots) → sessions → Map → table → Array."*

Everything in the interface exists to make that sentence, and anything that
does not contribute to it is decoration.

## Hint 2

Now the honesty requirements, because a detector that overclaims gets ignored
after its first false positive. Three things this tool cannot know:

- self size is not retained size, so the byte totals understate containers;
- one retainer path explains one instance;
- growth between two snapshots may be legitimate warm-up if the caller diffed
  the wrong pair.

A `verdict` of `"suspicious"` rather than `"leak"` for the borderline cases is
how you encode that uncertainty instead of hiding it.

## Hint 3

Think about where this runs. As a CLI over two files from production, it is a
debugging tool. Wired into CI — run the suite twice, snapshot, compare — it
becomes a regression test that catches leaks before they ship, and the
thresholds then need to be tight enough to be meaningful and loose enough to
be green on a normal day.

That difference in context is the argument for every threshold being an option
with a default rather than a constant.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review — weak references and their limits

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
export interface LivenessTracker {
  track(key: string, target: object): void;
  liveCount(): number;                 // after sweeping dead references
  isLive(key: string): boolean;
  sweep(): number;                     // returns how many dead entries were removed
  readonly tracked: number;            // entries still in the table, dead or not
}

export function createLivenessTracker(): LivenessTracker
```

Hold each target in a `WeakRef` so tracking never keeps it alive. `sweep()`
removes entries whose referent has been collected. `liveCount()` sweeps first,
then counts.

The gate only asserts the direction that is guaranteed: an object you are
still holding is always live. It does **not** assert that a dropped object
becomes dead, because nothing in the language promises when — or whether — a
collection happens.

Include a `FINALIZATION_CAVEAT` exported string of at least 120 characters
stating, in your own words, why a `FinalizationRegistry` must never be the
only thing that releases a resource.

```ts
const t = createLivenessTracker();
const held = {};
t.track("held", held);
t.isLive("held");     // true, always
```

```
uv run dojo test node v3nc04_memory_leaks review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`new WeakRef(target)` and `ref.deref()` are the whole API. `deref()` returns
the object or `undefined`, and the value can change between two calls — an
object alive on the first call may be gone on the second.

That is why `liveCount` sweeps before it counts rather than counting and
sweeping.

## Hint 2

```ts
const refs = new Map<string, WeakRef<object>>();
// sweep:
for (const [key, ref] of refs) if (ref.deref() === undefined) refs.delete(key);
```

Deleting from a `Map` while iterating it is defined and safe in JavaScript —
unlike an array, where removing an element shifts the ones you have not
visited. Worth knowing, because it makes this sweep a one-liner.

## Hint 3

The caveat string is not padding. Write it as if for a code reviewer: what
`FinalizationRegistry` promises (a callback, maybe, some time after
collection), what it does not (any timing, any ordering, running at all,
running at exit), and the consequence — a file handle or a socket closed only
from a finalizer leaks under exactly the conditions where it matters.

The decision left to you: whether `tracked` counts dead entries. It does, by
the spec above, and the gap between `tracked` and `liveCount()` is the useful
signal.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the guarantee boundary, because it is the whole reason this
exercise is a review rather than a build. Two statements:

- "an object I am still referencing is reachable" — guaranteed by the language;
- "an object I stopped referencing is collected" — guaranteed by nothing.

V8 collects when it decides to. It may keep a `WeakRef` target alive to the
end of the current job by design. A test asserting the second statement is a
test that fails on the machine you cannot reproduce.

## Hint 2

Now the practical use of `WeakRef`, which is narrower than people expect. It
is right for a cache where losing an entry is harmless — a memoisation table,
a parsed representation you can rebuild. It is wrong for anything where the
absence of the entry changes behaviour, because the absence is not under your
control.

The V8 team's own guidance amounts to: if you can express it with a `WeakMap`,
do that instead.

## Hint 3

Consider what a leak-hunting version of this tracker looks like in a real
service. Track every request context by id at creation; sweep every minute;
export `tracked - liveCount()` as a metric. A number that climbs means
contexts are being retained past their request, and unlike a heap snapshot it
costs nothing and runs continuously.

That is the useful shape: weak references as *instrumentation*, never as
lifetime management.
